questions.stem: Which histologic features are characteristic of dysplasia?
options: Pleomorphism with hyperchromatic nuclei and abnormal mitotic figures
Uniform small nuclei with no mitotic activity
Cell shrinkage with membrane blebbing and apoptotic bodies
Intact basement membrane with normal-appearing glandular architecture only
explanations: Correct. Dysplasia is disordered epithelial proliferation characterized by pleomorphism (variable cell/nuclear size and shape), abnormal hyperchromatic and enlarged nuclei, and abnormal mitotic figures; it is non-neoplastic but can be pre-cancerous, especially when severe.
Uniform small nuclei without mitotic activity describes normal or quiescent tissue, not the disordered, pleomorphic proliferation of dysplasia.
Cell shrinkage, membrane blebbing, and apoptotic bodies describe apoptosis, an unrelated process to the disordered proliferative changes of dysplasia.

Dysplasia is a description of abnormal cellular/nuclear morphology, and while carcinoma in situ (severe dysplasia) does not invade the basement membrane, normal-appearing architecture is not a feature of dysplasia itself.
questions.overview: Dysplasia refers to disordered, non-neoplastic epithelial proliferation featuring pleomorphism, hyperchromatic/enlarged nuclei, and abnormal mitotic figures. It typically follows hyperplasia or metaplasia, may be mild and reversible or severe and irreversible (carcinoma in situ, confined by the basement membrane), and can progress to invasive cancer.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman notices a firm, raised, pink scar that has grown beyond the original margins of an earlobe piercing site over several months. Biopsy shows disorganized bundles of type I and type III collagen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and its associated feature?
options: Granulation tissue, a normal transient stage of wound healing composed of proliferating fibroblasts and new capillaries
Keloid, which is more common at the earlobe and has a high recurrence rate after surgical excision
Fibrinoid necrosis, resulting from immune complex deposition in the dermal vessels
Dystrophic calcification secondary to prior localized tissue necrosis
Hypertrophic scar, which remains confined to the wound border and often regresses spontaneously
explanations: Granulation tissue is an early, transient stage of healing (3-5 days after injury) that eventually matures into scar; it does not describe a longstanding raised, expanding scar.

Correct. Keloids are raised scars that extend beyond the original wound borders, caused by excessive healing with more fibroblasts, growth factors, and disorganized type I and III collagen; they are especially common at the earlobe, deltoid, and upper back, and have a high recurrence rate if surgically removed.
Fibrinoid necrosis is a vascular lesion seen in autoimmune/immune complex disease (e.g., polyarteritis nodosa), not a feature of excessive dermal scarring.
Dystrophic calcification occurs in areas of prior necrosis with normal serum calcium and is unrelated to keloid formation.

Hypertrophic scars remain within the wound border and are composed mostly of parallel (organized) type III collagen — the opposite of this patient's findings of disorganized collagen extending beyond the wound margin.
questions.overview: Keloids are raised scars that grow beyond the original wound borders due to excessive fibroblast activity, growth factor signaling, and collagen (types I and III) deposition in a disorganized pattern. They are especially common at the earlobe, deltoid, and upper back, rare on palms/soles/eyelids, and tend to recur after surgical excision, in contrast to hypertrophic scars, which stay within wound borders and often regress.

questions.stem: Which of the following features distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?
options: Cell membrane remains intact and no inflammatory response is elicited
Cell swelling with membrane rupture
Random DNA fragmentation seen on gel electrophoresis
Always a pathologic process affecting many contiguous cells
explanations: Correct. Apoptosis is characterized by an intact cell membrane throughout the process (until the cell is consumed by phagocytes), which prevents leakage of cellular contents and therefore avoids triggering inflammation, unlike necrosis.
Cell swelling and membrane rupture are hallmarks of necrosis; apoptosis instead features cell shrinkage with an intact membrane.
Random DNA fragmentation is a feature of necrosis; apoptosis instead produces organized DNA laddering with fragments in multiples of 180-185 kbp.
Necrosis typically affects many cells and is always pathologic; apoptosis affects single cells and can be a normal physiologic process (e.g., embryogenesis, hormone withdrawal).
questions.overview: Apoptosis is an active, ATP-dependent, non-inflammatory form of programmed cell death in which the membrane stays intact, the cell shrinks, and DNA is cleaved into an orderly ladder pattern; it can be physiologic. Necrosis, in contrast, is an inflammatory process with membrane rupture, cell swelling, random DNA fragmentation, and is always pathologic, typically affecting many cells.

questions.stem: A patient with normal serum calcium levels has calcification identified within an area of prior tissue necrosis on imaging. This is best classified as which type of pathologic calcification?
options: Calciphylaxis
Nephrocalcinosis
Metastatic calcification
Dystrophic calcification
explanations: Calciphylaxis is a specific complication of chronic hyperphosphatemia in CKD causing vascular wall calcification and skin necrosis, not simply localized calcification with normal serum calcium.
Nephrocalcinosis refers specifically to calcium deposition in renal tubules due to hypercalcemia/hyperphosphatemia, not the generalized dystrophic pattern described here.
Metastatic calcification occurs in normal (non-necrotic) tissues and requires hypercalcemia and/or hyperphosphatemia, unlike this patient's normal calcium level and necrotic tissue location.

Correct. Dystrophic calcification is a local process that occurs in damaged/necrotic tissue despite normal serum calcium levels; damaged membrane phospholipids bind calcium and propagate microcrystal formation, seen in atherosclerotic vessels, damaged heart valves, and lung nodules.
questions.overview: Dystrophic calcification is a local process occurring in damaged or necrotic tissue (e.g., atherosclerotic vessels, damaged heart valves, chronic pancreatitis) despite normal serum calcium levels, driven by calcium binding to damaged membrane phospholipids. Metastatic calcification, in contrast, is a systemic process occurring in normal tissues (favoring acid-secreting tissues like gastric mucosa, kidney, lung) and requires hypercalcemia and/or hyperphosphatemia.

questions.stem: Unlike most other organs, which undergo coagulative necrosis after infarction, the brain characteristically undergoes which type of necrosis after an ischemic stroke?
options: Fibrinoid necrosis
Fat necrosis
Caseous necrosis
Liquefactive necrosis
explanations: Fibrinoid necrosis occurs in blood vessel walls due to immune complex deposition (e.g., polyarteritis nodosa), not in infarcted brain parenchyma.
Fat necrosis occurs in adipose tissue, classically from pancreatic lipases (acute pancreatitis) or trauma to fatty tissue such as breast, not brain infarction.
Caseous necrosis is a granulomatous, 'cheese-like' necrosis essentially specific to tuberculosis infection, not the typical pattern after brain infarction.

Correct. The brain is a key exception to the typical pattern of infarction: unlike the myocardium, kidney, or spleen (which undergo coagulative necrosis), the brain undergoes liquefactive necrosis after ischemic infarction, in which tissue is broken down into a liquid mass by enzymes.
questions.overview: Most solid organs (myocardium, kidney, spleen) undergo coagulative necrosis after infarction, in which tissue architecture is preserved for days because enzymes are also damaged, limiting proteolysis. The brain is a key exception: ischemic brain infarction undergoes liquefactive necrosis, in which tissue is broken down into a liquid mass, a pattern also seen in bacterial/fungal abscesses.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has a history of recurrent pneumonia, suppurative lymphadenitis, and a hepatic abscess. Cultures from the abscess grow Staphylococcus aureus, and prior infections have included Serratia marcescens and Aspergillus. Biopsy of affected tissue shows granuloma formation. A nitroblue tetrazolium test is abnormal. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient's phagocytes?
options: Catalase
Myeloperoxidase
NADPH oxidase
Glutathione peroxidase
Superoxide dismutase
explanations: Catalase deficiency is not a human immunodeficiency described in these notes; rather, catalase-positive organisms are the pathogens that cause infection in CGD because they degrade the H2O2 phagocytes would otherwise use.

Myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 to HOCl in the last step of the respiratory burst; its deficiency causes a milder, often subclinical phenotype, not the classic recurrent catalase-positive infections described here.

Correct. Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in NADPH oxidase, preventing phagocytes from generating superoxide/H2O2 during the respiratory burst; catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus) destroy their own H2O2, leaving phagocytes without usable peroxide to kill them, and granulomas form as infection persists.
Glutathione peroxidase deficiency is not associated with this presentation; glutathione-dependent free radical inactivation is instead relevant to G6PD deficiency and RBC hemolysis.
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to H2O2 and is not the enzyme deficient in CGD.
questions.overview: Chronic granulomatous disease results from NADPH oxidase deficiency, which prevents the respiratory burst (superoxide → H2O2) that phagocytes normally use with myeloperoxidase to kill bacteria. Because catalase-negative organisms generate their own H2O2 that phagocytes can still exploit, CGD patients are susceptible specifically to catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Pseudomonas, Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus), and chronic infection drives granuloma formation.

questions.stem: Opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, triggered by calcium, results in which of the following?
options: Formation of DNA laddering
Increased ATP synthesis via enhanced electron transport
Loss of membrane potential and failure of oxidative phosphorylation
Activation of Toll-like receptors
explanations: DNA laddering is a feature of apoptosis via caspase-mediated cleavage, not a direct consequence of mitochondrial pore opening described under mechanisms of cell injury.
Pore opening impairs, rather than enhances, oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis.

Correct. The mitochondrial permeability transition pore is opened by calcium, causing loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and failure of oxidative phosphorylation, contributing to ATP depletion and cell injury.
TLR activation is a pattern-recognition receptor process unrelated to mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening.
questions.overview: Mitochondrial damage is a key mechanism of cell injury, often resulting from lack of oxygen or reactive oxygen species. Calcium opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, causing loss of membrane potential and failure of oxidative phosphorylation, which compounds ATP depletion and drives the cell toward irreversible injury.

questions.stem: Chronic cigarette smoking classically causes which epithelial change in the trachea and bronchi?
options: Replacement of ciliated columnar epithelium with stratified squamous epithelium
Increase in size of individual ciliated columnar cells
Increase in cell number of the native ciliated columnar epithelium
Replacement of squamous epithelium with columnar epithelium
explanations: Correct. Chronic irritation from smoking causes squamous metaplasia, the most common type, in which the normal ciliated columnar epithelium of the trachea/bronchi is replaced by more durable stratified squamous epithelium; the trade-off is loss of cilia, increasing vulnerability to infection.
An increase in individual cell size describes hypertrophy, not the phenotypic change (metaplasia) that occurs in smokers' airway epithelium.
An increase in cell number without a change in cell type would be hyperplasia, not the metaplastic change (change in cell type) seen with smoking.
Replacement of squamous with columnar epithelium describes Barrett's esophagus (a response to acid), the opposite direction of change seen in smokers' airways.
questions.overview: Metaplasia is a reversible change in cell phenotype allowing tissue to better withstand a chronic stressor. In smokers, the normal ciliated columnar epithelium of the trachea and bronchi undergoes squamous metaplasia (the most common type of metaplasia) because squamous epithelium is more durable, though the loss of cilia impairs clearance and increases infection risk; metaplasia can progress to dysplasia and malignancy.

questions.stem: Left ventricular hypertrophy in response to chronic hypertension occurs via which cellular adaptation, and why does this adaptation (rather than hyperplasia) predominate in cardiac muscle?
options: Metaplasia, because cardiac tissue changes phenotype under pressure overload
Hyperplasia, because cardiac myocytes divide readily in response to increased workload
Atrophy, because increased workload reduces myocyte size
Hypertrophy, because cardiac myocytes are permanent/terminally differentiated cells incapable of significant division
explanations: Metaplasia describes a change in epithelial cell phenotype in response to a stressor (e.g., squamous metaplasia in smokers' airways), not the myocardial response to pressure overload.
Hyperplasia (increase in cell number) occurs in tissues capable of division, such as epithelial cells; cardiac myocytes cannot meaningfully proliferate, so hypertrophy, not hyperplasia, dominates.
Atrophy is a decrease, not increase, in cell size and is not the response to increased hemodynamic workload.

Correct. Cardiac myocytes are permanent (terminally differentiated, G0) cells with essentially no capacity for division, so they respond to increased workload (e.g., hypertension) with hypertrophy — an increase in cell size with more proteins and filaments — rather than hyperplasia.
questions.overview: Permanent (terminally differentiated) tissues such as cardiac myocytes, skeletal muscle, and neurons are essentially non-dividing and therefore respond to increased demand with hypertrophy (increased cell size) rather than hyperplasia. Left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension is a classic pathologic example, in contrast to physiologic hypertrophy such as pregnancy-related uterine growth.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old African American woman presents with dyspnea and is found to have bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest imaging. Serum calcium is elevated with appropriately suppressed PTH. Lymph node biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells. Which of the following best explains her hypercalcemia?
options: TNF-alpha directly increases renal calcium reabsorption
Chronic granulomatous inflammation causes decreased urinary calcium excretion via tubular injury
Ectopic PTH secretion by epithelioid macrophages
Granuloma cells secrete PTH-related peptide, mimicking primary hyperparathyroidism
Activated macrophages within granulomas express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, increasing conversion of 25-OH vitamin D to active calcitriol
explanations: TNF-alpha maintains granulomatous inflammation but is not described as directly increasing renal calcium reabsorption.
The mechanism described in the notes is increased vitamin D activation by macrophages, not decreased urinary excretion from tubular injury.
PTH is suppressed (not ectopically secreted) in granulomatous hypercalcemia; the mechanism is macrophage-driven vitamin D activation, not PTH secretion.
PTH-related peptide is a mechanism of hypercalcemia of malignancy, not the mechanism described for granulomatous disease in these notes.

Correct. In sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases, activated macrophages within granulomas have high 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, increasing conversion of 25-OH vitamin D to active calcitriol (1,25-OH2 vitamin D) independent of renal/PTH regulation, raising serum calcium.
questions.overview: Granulomatous diseases such as sarcoidosis can cause hypercalcemia because activated macrophages within granulomas possess high 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, converting 25-OH vitamin D to its active form (calcitriol) independent of the kidney's normal PTH-regulated control, raising serum calcium and often suppressing PTH.

questions.stem: Which enzyme, found in mitochondria, converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide as part of normal free radical inactivation?
options: Superoxide dismutase
Catalase
Glutathione peroxidase
Myeloperoxidase
explanations: Correct. Superoxide dismutase, located in mitochondria, converts superoxide (O2·) to the more stable hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), an early step in free radical inactivation.
Catalase, located in peroxisomes, converts H2O2 to water, acting downstream of superoxide dismutase rather than converting superoxide itself.
Glutathione peroxidase, located in the cytoplasm and requiring glutathione, also converts H2O2 to water, but does not act on superoxide directly.
Myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 to hypochlorous acid during the phagocyte respiratory burst, a bactericidal function distinct from generalized cellular free radical inactivation.
questions.overview: Free radicals are generated at low levels during normal metabolism and inactivated by a coordinated enzyme system: superoxide dismutase (mitochondria) converts superoxide to H2O2, which is then converted to water by catalase (peroxisomes) or glutathione peroxidase (cytoplasm, requires glutathione). Overwhelming this system leads to cell injury.

questions.stem: Fibrinoid necrosis of blood vessel walls, seen classically in polyarteritis nodosa, results from which underlying process?
options: Caseous breakdown of mycobacterial infection
Loss of blood supply causing coagulative necrosis of the vessel wall
Saponification of fat by pancreatic lipases
Deposition of antibody-antigen immune complexes in the vessel wall (type III hypersensitivity)
explanations: Caseous necrosis is the mycobacterial granulomatous pattern seen in tuberculosis, an entirely different necrosis type from vascular fibrinoid necrosis.
Coagulative necrosis from ischemia is a distinct process from the immune complex-mediated fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls.
Saponification of fat by lipases describes fat necrosis (e.g., acute pancreatitis), not the immune complex-mediated vascular process of fibrinoid necrosis.

Correct. Fibrinoid necrosis occurs when antibody-antigen immune complexes deposit in vessel walls (a type III hypersensitivity reaction), causing fibrin to leak into the vessel wall, appearing pink on microscopy; it is classically seen in polyarteritis nodosa, presenting with purpura, renal failure, neuropathy, and severe hypertension.
questions.overview: Fibrinoid necrosis occurs in blood vessel walls and is visible only microscopically (no gross findings), resulting from deposition of antibody-antigen immune complexes (type III hypersensitivity), which causes fibrin to leak into the vessel wall. Polyarteritis nodosa is the classic associated disorder, presenting with purpura, renal failure, neuropathy, and severe hypertension/preeclampsia.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a 15-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease undergoes upper endoscopy for surveillance. Salmon-colored mucosa is noted in the distal esophagus, and biopsy reveals columnar epithelium with goblet cells replacing the normal stratified squamous epithelium. Which of the following best describes this process and its clinical significance?
options: Dysplasia, an irreversible pre-malignant change with pleomorphic nuclei already present
Hypertrophy, an increase in cell size of the esophageal epithelium in response to acid stress
Hyperplasia, an increase in the number of squamous cells without change in cell type
Metaplasia, a potentially reversible adaptive change that carries increased risk of progression to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma
Anaplasia, undifferentiated growth indicating a fully malignant transformation has already occurred
explanations: Dysplasia is a distinct, more advanced step characterized by pleomorphism and abnormal nuclei that may follow metaplasia; the biopsy described (columnar epithelium replacing squamous epithelium) is the metaplastic change itself, not dysplasia.
Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, not a change in epithelial cell type, and does not describe Barrett's esophagus.
Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number of the same cell type; this biopsy shows a change in cell type (squamous to columnar), which defines metaplasia, not hyperplasia.

Correct. This is Barrett's esophagus, a classic example of metaplasia in which chronic gastric acid exposure (the stressor) causes normal stratified squamous esophageal epithelium to convert to more acid-resistant columnar (intestinal-type) epithelium; metaplasia is potentially reversible but can progress to dysplasia and malignancy (esophageal adenocarcinoma).
Anaplasia describes undifferentiated, malignant cell growth; Barrett's esophagus is a benign (though pre-malignant) metaplastic change, not anaplasia.
questions.overview: Barrett's esophagus is the classic example of metaplasia: chronic gastric acid exposure causes normal stratified squamous esophageal epithelium to be replaced by more acid-resistant columnar (intestinal-type) epithelium with goblet cells. Metaplasia is a potentially reversible adaptive response to stress, but it can progress through dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma, warranting endoscopic surveillance.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean descent develops jaundice, dark urine, and back pain two days after eating a meal containing fava beans. Peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of his hemolysis?
options: Excess hepcidin traps iron within red cell precursors
Deficient NADPH oxidase impairs the respiratory burst in red cells
Fenton reaction from iron overload directly lyses red cells
Depletion of glutathione impairs neutralization of free radicals, causing oxidative damage to red blood cells
Overexpression of BCL-2 prevents red cell apoptosis
explanations: Hepcidin regulates iron transport via ferroportin and is unrelated to G6PD-mediated hemolysis.
NADPH oxidase and the respiratory burst are functions of phagocytes (relevant to CGD), not the mechanism of G6PD-deficient RBC hemolysis, which instead involves impaired glutathione regeneration.
The Fenton reaction (relevant to hemochromatosis/Wilson disease) generates hydroxyl radicals from transition metals, not the mechanism described for fava bean-induced hemolysis.

Correct. G6PD deficiency limits the supply of NADPH needed to regenerate glutathione; compounds in fava beans (vicine, converted to divicine) generate reactive oxygen species that deplete the limited glutathione reserve, causing oxidative damage and hemolysis of red blood cells.
BCL-2 overexpression is the mechanism in follicular lymphoma, not G6PD deficiency-related hemolysis.
questions.overview: G6PD deficiency limits the cell's supply of glutathione, the key antioxidant that neutralizes free radicals in red blood cells via glutathione peroxidase. Oxidative stressors such as fava beans (via vicine/divicine) overwhelm this limited reserve, causing free radical damage and hemolysis, classically producing bite cells and Heinz bodies.

questions.stem: Cellular (hydropic) swelling, a major feature of reversible cell injury, is primarily caused by dysfunction of which cellular component?
options: Lysosomal enzymes
Telomerase
Caspase enzymes
Na+/K+ ATPase pumps
explanations: Lysosomal enzyme release causes degradation of cellular contents in irreversible injury (necrosis), not the swelling of early reversible injury.
Telomerase relates to chromosome end maintenance and replicative capacity, unrelated to acute cellular swelling.
Caspase enzymes drive apoptosis, a distinct process from the reversible hydropic swelling described here.

Correct. Reversible cell injury commonly features cellular swelling (hydropic change, water accumulation) due to decreased Na+/K+ ATPase pump activity, impairing the cell's ability to maintain normal ion and water gradients.
questions.overview: Cellular swelling (hydropic change) is a major feature of reversible cell injury, resulting from decreased Na+/K+ ATPase pump activity that impairs the cell's ability to regulate water and ion balance. Other reversible changes include fatty change, mitochondrial swelling, membrane blebbing, ER dilation, and ribosome detachment from the ER (polysomal detachment) with decreased protein synthesis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man on chronic lisinopril therapy for hypertension presents to the emergency department with acute swelling of his lips and tongue without urticaria or pruritus. There is no known allergen exposure. Which of the following mediators is most likely responsible for his presentation?
options: C1 inhibitor deficiency causing unopposed complement activation
Serotonin, released from activated platelets
Leukotriene C4, synthesized via the lipoxygenase pathway
Histamine, released from IgE-sensitized mast cells
Bradykinin, due to decreased degradation by angiotensin converting enzyme
explanations: C1 inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, a separate cause of bradykinin excess (also degraded by C1 inhibitor), but this patient's presentation is explained by ACE inhibitor use, not a hereditary enzyme deficiency.
Serotonin is a vasoactive amine from platelets/mast cells involved in vasodilation but is not the mediator implicated in ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema.
Leukotrienes increase vascular permeability but are not the specific mediator elevated by ACE inhibition; bradykinin is the mediator degraded by ACE.

IgE-mediated mast cell histamine release typically produces urticaria/pruritus, which this patient lacks; his presentation on ACE inhibitor therapy is classic for bradykinin-mediated, not histamine-mediated, angioedema.

Correct. Bradykinin is normally degraded by ACE; ACE inhibitors reduce bradykinin degradation, raising bradykinin levels, which causes vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and angioedema — a well-described dangerous side effect distinct from an allergic/histamine-mediated reaction.
questions.overview: Bradykinin is a vasodilator that increases vascular permeability and causes pain; it is normally degraded by ACE and by C1 inhibitor. ACE inhibitors can raise bradykinin levels, causing angioedema — a dangerous side effect distinct from IgE/histamine-mediated allergic reactions — while C1 inhibitor deficiency causes a separate condition, hereditary angioedema, via the same bradykinin pathway.

questions.stem: Toll-like receptors on macrophages are pattern recognition receptors that respond to which of the following?
options: Only antibody Fc fragments
Only complement C3b bound to bacteria
PAMPs and DAMPs
Only self-antigens presented on MHC I
explanations: Fc receptor engagement by antibodies is a distinct macrophage activation pathway from TLR-mediated PAMP/DAMP recognition.
Complement and Fc receptor engagement are separate, additional activators of macrophages mentioned in the notes, but TLRs specifically recognize PAMPs/DAMPs, not complement fragments exclusively.

Correct. Toll-like receptors recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, found on microbes but not human cells) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, released only during tissue damage, such as mitochondrial proteins/DNA), triggering cytokine secretion and inflammation.
MHC I antigen presentation is unrelated to TLR pattern recognition; TLRs recognize PAMPs/DAMPs, not self-antigen/MHC I complexes.
questions.overview: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are pattern recognition receptors on macrophages, dendritic cells, and other cells found on the cell membrane and endosomes. They recognize PAMPs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns present on microbes but not human cells) and DAMPs (damage-associated molecular patterns released only during tissue injury, e.g., mitochondrial DNA/proteins), triggering cytokine secretion and initiating the acute inflammatory response.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with massive, non-tender lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and chronic autoimmune cytopenias. Flow cytometry shows an expanded population of CD4-/CD8- double-negative T cells. Family history is notable for lymphoma. Genetic testing is expected to reveal a defect in which apoptotic pathway?
options: NADPH oxidase-mediated respiratory burst
Extrinsic (death receptor) pathway involving FAS and FAS ligand
p53-mediated cell cycle arrest
Cytochrome c binding to APAF-1
Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway involving BCL-2 and BAX
explanations: NADPH oxidase relates to the respiratory burst in phagocytes (as in CGD), not to lymphocyte apoptosis or ALPS.

Correct. This is autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS), caused by a defective FAS-FAS ligand (extrinsic/death-receptor) pathway, which normally eliminates self-reactive T cells during thymic negative selection; impaired extrinsic apoptosis leads to lymphocyte overproduction, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, autoimmunity, and high lymphoma risk.
p53-mediated arrest relates to DNA damage responses and the intrinsic pathway, not the FAS-mediated defect described in ALPS.
Cytochrome c/APAF-1 binding is part of the intrinsic pathway; ALPS involves failure of the extrinsic FAS pathway.

The intrinsic pathway (BCL-2/BAX/BAK, cytochrome c) governs mitochondria-triggered apoptosis from growth factor withdrawal or DNA damage; ALPS is specifically a defect of the extrinsic FAS pathway, not this pathway.
questions.overview: Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) results from a defective FAS-FAS ligand extrinsic apoptotic pathway, which normally kills self-reactive T cells in the thymic medulla (negative selection) and downregulates immune responses after infection resolves. Poor negative selection leads to lymphocyte overproduction, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, autoimmune disease, and an increased risk of lymphoma.

questions.stem: Which receptor-ligand interaction is characteristic of the extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway of apoptosis and is used during thymic negative selection?
options: BAX binding BCL-2
Cytochrome c binding APAF-1
TLR binding PAMPs
FAS (CD95) binding FAS ligand
explanations: BAX binding to anti-apoptotic proteins like BCL-2 is part of the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway, not the extrinsic death-receptor pathway.
Cytochrome c binding APAF-1 is a key step of the intrinsic pathway, occurring after mitochondrial pore opening, not the extrinsic pathway.
TLR-PAMP binding activates macrophages/innate immune cytokine release, unrelated to death-receptor-mediated apoptosis.

Correct. FAS (CD95) is a death receptor of the TNF receptor family; binding of FAS ligand triggers a caspase activation cascade, and this FAS-FAS ligand interaction is used to eliminate self-reactive T cells in the thymic medulla during negative selection.
questions.overview: The extrinsic (death-receptor) apoptotic pathway is triggered by membrane death receptors of the TNF receptor family, the best-described being FAS (CD95), which binds FAS ligand to activate caspases. This pathway mediates killing of virus-infected cells by CD8 T cells (via Fas ligand) and eliminates self-reactive T cells during thymic negative selection; its failure causes autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after intentionally ingesting a large quantity of acetaminophen 36 hours ago. She now has right upper quadrant pain and markedly elevated AST/ALT. The hepatotoxic metabolite responsible for her liver injury is generated by which hepatic enzyme system and causes damage by which mechanism?
options: Myeloperoxidase converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid, damaging hepatocyte membranes
Cytochrome P450 generates NAPQI, a reactive oxygen species that causes free radical-mediated lipid peroxidation
Lysyl oxidase cross-links hepatic collagen, causing fibrosis
Xanthine oxidase generates uric acid, activating the inflammasome
Superoxide dismutase overactivity depletes cellular H2O2 stores
explanations: Myeloperoxidase functions in phagocyte respiratory burst, not in hepatic drug metabolism/toxicity.

Correct. Acetaminophen is metabolized by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (phase 1 metabolism) to NAPQI, a reactive oxygen species; NAPQI causes free radical liver damage including lipid peroxidation of hepatocyte membranes, leading to hepatotoxicity in overdose.
Lysyl oxidase is involved in wound healing collagen cross-linking, unrelated to acetaminophen's hepatotoxic mechanism.
Xanthine oxidase and inflammasome/uric acid activation are not the mechanism described for acetaminophen toxicity in the notes.
Superoxide dismutase inactivates free radicals; overactivity is not the described mechanism of acetaminophen-induced liver damage, which is instead driven by the toxic metabolite NAPQI itself.
questions.overview: Acetaminophen is metabolized by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes to NAPQI, a reactive oxygen species that causes free radical liver damage (including lipid peroxidation) when glutathione stores are overwhelmed, as in overdose. This is a classic example of drug metabolism generating a bioactive free radical intermediate.

questions.stem: Malignant cells achieve unlimited replicative potential ('immortality') primarily through upregulation of which enzyme, which is normally active mainly in stem cells?
options: Cytochrome P450
Metalloproteinase
Telomerase
Lysyl oxidase
explanations: Cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolize drugs and xenobiotics, unrelated to telomere maintenance or cancer cell immortality.
Metalloproteinases are zinc-containing enzymes that degrade extracellular matrix during wound healing/remodeling and tumor invasion, but are not the enzyme responsible for replicative immortality.

Correct. Normal somatic cells undergo only 60-70 divisions before becoming senescent due to progressive telomere shortening; telomerase prevents this loss of genetic material with each duplication and is normally active mainly in stem cells, but is upregulated in almost all cancers, conferring unlimited replicative potential — a hallmark of malignancy.
Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen during wound healing, unrelated to telomere maintenance or replicative capacity.
questions.overview: Normal cells are capable of only about 60-70 divisions before becoming senescent due to telomere shortening with each replication. Telomerase, an enzyme normally active mainly in stem cells, prevents this loss of genetic material; its upregulation in nearly all cancers confers unlimited replicative potential ('immortality'), one of the key hallmarks of malignant cells alongside autonomous growth, apoptosis evasion, immune evasion, angiogenesis, and invasive/metastatic ability.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with an ST-elevation myocardial infarction and undergoes emergent percutaneous coronary intervention with restoration of coronary blood flow. Despite successful reperfusion, additional myocardial injury occurs after flow is restored. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this paradoxical injury?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure causes transudative pulmonary edema
Persistent complete absence of blood flow leads to ongoing coagulative necrosis
Dystrophic calcification of infarcted myocardium
Fibrinoid necrosis of the coronary vessel wall from immune complex deposition
Reintroduction of oxygen generates free radicals in previously ischemic, antioxidant-depleted tissue with damaged mitochondria
explanations: Transudative pulmonary edema relates to hydrostatic pressure changes (e.g., heart failure), not the free radical-mediated mechanism of myocardial reperfusion injury.
Reperfusion injury specifically requires restoration of blood flow; ongoing injury from persistent absence of flow describes ischemia itself, not the paradoxical reperfusion phenomenon.
Dystrophic calcification may occur later in areas of prior necrosis but does not explain the acute paradoxical injury seen upon reperfusion.
Fibrinoid necrosis is an immune complex-mediated vascular process (e.g., polyarteritis nodosa), unrelated to reperfusion injury mechanics.

Correct. Reperfusion injury occurs because reintroduction of oxygen after ischemia generates free radicals, antioxidants have been depleted during the ischemic injury, and damaged mitochondria incompletely reduce oxygen, all producing reactive oxygen species that injure cells that might otherwise have recovered.
questions.overview: Reperfusion injury occurs when blood flow is restored to previously ischemic tissue (e.g., after MI). While some reversibly injured cells recover, others are paradoxically damaged by a burst of free radical generation from reintroduced oxygen, loss of antioxidants during the ischemic period, and damaged mitochondria incompletely reducing oxygen.

questions.stem: In the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis, which proteins promote apoptosis by opening pores in the mitochondrial membrane to release cytochrome c?
options: MCL1
FAS and FAS ligand
BCL-2 and BCL-XL
BAX and BAK
explanations: MCL1 is also an anti-apoptotic BCL2-family protein found in the mitochondrial membrane, preventing (not promoting) cytochrome c release.
FAS and FAS ligand are death receptor components of the extrinsic pathway, not the mitochondrial pore-forming proteins of the intrinsic pathway.
BCL-2 and BCL-XL are anti-apoptotic proteins that prevent cytochrome c release by keeping mitochondrial pores closed — the opposite function of BAX/BAK.

Correct. BAX and BAK are pro-apoptotic BCL2-family proteins that bind anti-apoptotic proteins and open pores in the mitochondrial membrane, allowing cytochrome c release, which binds APAF-1 and activates caspases.
questions.overview: The intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathway is controlled by the balance of BCL2-family proteins: anti-apoptotic members (BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL1) keep mitochondrial pores closed, while pro-apoptotic members (BAX, BAK) open these pores to release cytochrome c, which binds APAF-1 to activate caspases and trigger apoptosis.

questions.stem: In patients with hemochromatosis, excess free iron contributes to cell injury primarily through which reaction?
options: DNA laddering via caspase-mediated cleavage
The Warburg effect, generating lactate from glucose
The respiratory burst, generating hypochlorous acid
The Fenton reaction, generating hydroxyl radicals from hydrogen peroxide
explanations: DNA laddering is a feature of apoptosis, not the mechanism of iron-mediated free radical tissue injury in hemochromatosis.
The Warburg effect describes cancer cell metabolism (aerobic glycolysis), unrelated to iron-catalyzed free radical generation.
The respiratory burst is a phagocyte bactericidal mechanism, not the mechanism by which excess iron causes tissue injury in hemochromatosis.

Correct. In hemochromatosis (iron overload) and Wilson disease (copper overload), excess transition metals catalyze the Fenton reaction, converting H2O2 into the highly reactive hydroxyl radical (OH·), which causes significant free radical-mediated tissue damage.
questions.overview: Transition metals like iron and copper catalyze the Fenton reaction, converting hydrogen peroxide into the highly reactive hydroxyl radical, which causes cell injury via lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, and DNA damage. This mechanism underlies tissue damage in iron overload (hemochromatosis) and copper overload (Wilson disease), conditions in which normal metal storage/transport proteins (transferrin, ferritin, ceruloplasmin) are overwhelmed.

questions.stem: In the typical timeline of acute inflammation, which cell type predominates within the first 24-48 hours before being replaced by a longer-lived cell type?
options: Macrophages
Neutrophils
Lymphocytes
Eosinophils
explanations: Macrophages/monocytes dominate later (after about 2 days) because they live longer and can replicate in tissue, not in the initial 24-48 hour window.

Correct. Neutrophils dominate the first 24-48 hours of acute inflammation because they attach firmly to adhesion molecules early and are abundant in the bloodstream, but they undergo apoptosis after 24-48 hours.
Lymphocytes typically appear first in viral infections, an exception to the typical bacterial-injury timeline, not the general rule.
Eosinophils dominate in hypersensitivity reactions, an exception to the typical timeline, not the default early responder.
questions.overview: Acute inflammation follows a typical cellular timeline: neutrophils dominate in the first 24-48 hours (short-lived, quick to arrive) and then undergo apoptosis, while monocytes/macrophages become dominant after about 2 days because they live longer and can proliferate in tissue. Exceptions include Pseudomonas infection (prolonged neutrophil dominance), viral infections (early lymphocytes), and hypersensitivity reactions (eosinophils).

questions.stem: A gel electrophoresis pattern showing DNA fragments in regular multiples of approximately 180-185 kbp, forming a 'ladder,' is characteristic of which process?
options: Apoptosis
Dystrophic calcification
Metaplasia
Necrosis
explanations: Correct. Apoptotic caspases cleave DNA at specific internucleosomal regions, producing fragments in regular multiples of 180-185 kbp that form a characteristic 'ladder' pattern on gel electrophoresis.
Dystrophic calcification is a calcium deposition process in necrotic tissue and has no relationship to DNA fragmentation patterns.
Metaplasia is a change in cell phenotype, not a DNA fragmentation pattern, and is unrelated to gel electrophoresis findings.
Necrosis produces random, non-uniform DNA fragmentation, which does not create a discrete ladder pattern on gel electrophoresis.
questions.overview: DNA laddering is a hallmark laboratory finding of apoptosis: caspases cleave chromosomal DNA at regular intervals, producing fragments in multiples of 180-185 kbp that appear as a discrete ladder on gel electrophoresis. This contrasts with necrosis, in which DNA is degraded randomly, producing a smear rather than a ladder.

questions.stem: Activation of the cytosolic inflammasome by uric acid, extracellular ATP, or free DNA primarily leads to production of which cytokine?
options: IL-4
TGF-beta
IFN-gamma
IL-1
explanations: IL-4 is produced by T cells and drives alternative (M2) macrophage activation for tissue repair, not the inflammasome pathway.
TGF-beta promotes healing/scar formation and is anti-inflammatory, not a product of inflammasome activation.
IFN-gamma drives classical (M1) macrophage activation from T cells, not inflammasome activation.

Correct. The inflammasome is a cytosolic protein complex activated by components of damaged cells (uric acid, extracellular ATP, free DNA) that leads to production of IL-1 and release of inflammatory mediators.
questions.overview: The inflammasome is a cytosolic protein complex present in many cells that senses markers of cellular damage — uric acid, extracellular ATP, and free DNA — and, once activated, drives production of IL-1 and release of other inflammatory mediators, linking cell damage recognition to the innate inflammatory response.

questions.stem: Increased intracellular calcium contributes to cell injury primarily by activating which class of enzymes that break down membrane phospholipids?
options: Lysyl oxidase
Metalloproteinases
Cytochrome P450 enzymes
Calcium-dependent phospholipases
explanations: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent enzyme that cross-links collagen during wound healing, unrelated to calcium-mediated cell injury.
Metalloproteinases are zinc-containing enzymes that degrade extracellular matrix proteins during wound healing/remodeling, not the intracellular calcium-driven injury mechanism.
Cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolize drugs and can generate free radical intermediates, but they are not the calcium-activated enzymes that degrade membrane phospholipids.

Correct. Calcium influx is a hallmark of cell injury; increased intracellular calcium activates calcium-dependent phospholipases, which break down membrane phospholipids and damage mitochondria, contributing to cellular injury.
questions.overview: Calcium is normally maintained at very low intracellular concentrations; injury causes calcium influx across the cell membrane and release from intracellular stores, a hallmark of cell injury. Elevated calcium activates calcium-dependent phospholipases that break down membrane phospholipids and damage mitochondria, contributing to progression toward irreversible injury.

questions.stem: During the phagocyte respiratory burst, which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid to kill engulfed bacteria?
options: Catalase
Myeloperoxidase
Superoxide dismutase
NADPH oxidase
explanations: Catalase breaks down H2O2 to water and is a free radical inactivation enzyme, not the enzyme generating the bactericidal hypochlorous acid in phagocytes.

Correct. Myeloperoxidase catalyzes the conversion of H2O2 (combined with chloride) to hypochlorous acid (HOCl), a potent bactericidal agent, in the final step of the respiratory burst within the phagosome.
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to H2O2, an intermediate step, not the enzyme that generates hypochlorous acid.
NADPH oxidase generates superoxide from oxygen as the first step of the respiratory burst, upstream of myeloperoxidase's action on H2O2.
questions.overview: The respiratory burst allows phagocytes to kill engulfed bacteria within the phagosome using three key enzymes in sequence: NADPH oxidase generates superoxide from oxygen, superoxide dismutase converts this to H2O2, and myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 (with chloride) to bactericidal hypochlorous acid. Chronic granulomatous disease results from NADPH oxidase deficiency, disabling this pathway.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with painless, waxing-and-waning cervical lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows a nodular proliferation of small cleaved lymphocytes, and cytogenetics reveal t(14;18). Immunohistochemical staining shows marked overexpression of an anti-apoptotic protein normally located in the mitochondrial membrane. Which of the following best explains how this overexpression contributes to lymphomagenesis?
options: It upregulates FAS ligand expression, promoting extrinsic apoptosis of malignant cells
It inactivates p53, allowing accumulation of DNA damage
It activates caspase-9 directly, accelerating programmed cell death
It prevents opening of mitochondrial membrane pores, blocking cytochrome c release and caspase activation
It increases telomerase activity, shortening telomeres with each division
explanations: FAS ligand upregulation would promote, not prevent, extrinsic apoptosis; BCL-2 overexpression instead blocks the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway and has no described role in FAS ligand expression.
The notes describe BCL-2 overexpression, not p53 inactivation, as the mechanism in follicular lymphoma.
BCL-2 is anti-apoptotic and inhibits, not activates, caspase activation.

Correct. Follicular lymphoma's t(14;18) translocation places BCL-2 under the IgH promoter, causing BCL-2 overexpression; BCL-2 sits in the mitochondrial membrane and prevents pore opening/cytochrome c release, so caspases are never activated via the intrinsic pathway and malignant B cells fail to undergo apoptosis, leading to uncontrolled accumulation.
Telomerase increases telomere maintenance (not shortening) and is a separate hallmark of malignancy unrelated to the BCL-2 mechanism described for follicular lymphoma.
questions.overview: Follicular lymphoma is a B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma driven by BCL-2 overexpression from the t(14;18) translocation. BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic mitochondrial membrane protein that normally prevents cytochrome c release; its overexpression keeps mitochondrial pores closed so caspases cannot be activated via the intrinsic pathway, resulting in evasion of apoptosis and uncontrolled lymphocyte accumulation.
